Adult Guadalupe bass (Micropterus treculii) attain a maximum recorded total length of 45.2 centimeters [Li = 45.2 centimeters], a value derived from a standard length of 38 centimeters using the species-specific length conversion factor F2. This ultimate total length, which represents the largest individuals observed in riverine populations, corresponds to a substantial ultimate wet weight of 1.58 kilograms [Wwi = 1.58 kilograms], estimated from the species' length-weight relationship. In contrast, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva, which measures just over two millimeters in egg diameter before hatching, begins exogenous feeding at a remarkably low wet weight at birth of 0.0054 grams [Wwb = 0.0054 grams]. This minute initial mass, typical of centrarchid larvae, highlights the enormous disparity between the larval and adult body sizes that characterizes the life history of this endemic Texas black bass.

Puberty in Guadalupe bass occurs at a notably small body size relative to the species' ultimate dimensions. The total length at puberty is 8.3 centimeters [Lp = 8.3 centimeters], corresponding to a standard length of approximately 7 centimeters when applying the same conversion factor F2. This early attainment of sexual maturity, at roughly 18 percent of the maximum total length, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive output over extended somatic growth. The wet weight at puberty that accompanies this length is 9.8 grams [Wwp = 9.8 grams], a value predicted from the conspecific length-weight relationship. Such a modest body mass at the onset of gonadal maturation is consistent with patterns observed in other small-bodied centrarchids inhabiting thermally variable headwater streams.

Reproductive output in Guadalupe bass has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. At this thermal regime, females measuring 24.2 centimeters in standard length, or approximately 28.8 centimeters in total length, produce a clutch size of approximately 9286 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 9286 eggs per spawning event], and they complete roughly one spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per year] under the same thermal conditions. This annual reproductive allocation is substantial for a fish of this size and reflects the high fecundity typical of iteroparous black basses. The temperature used in these observations represents a moderate thermal regime that supports active feeding and gametogenesis in this species.

The lifespan of Guadalupe bass, measured as time since birth at death in wild populations, reaches approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days] at a mean annual water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This maximum longevity of roughly six years is relatively short compared to some congeneric species, such as Micropterus salmoides, which can exceed a decade in favorable habitats. The constrained lifespan may be linked to the species' endemic distribution in the thermally fluctuating and hydrologically unpredictable rivers of central Texas. At the population level, this limited longevity, combined with the early onset of puberty at 8.3 centimeters [Lp = 8.3 centimeters] total length, produces a life history that emphasizes early and high fecundity to offset adult mortality.

Field surveys of Guadalupe bass in the Llano River system have provided additional context for the species' body size metrics. Although individuals can reach an ultimate total length of 45.2 centimeters [Li = 45.2 centimeters] in optimal habitat, most adults encountered during electrofishing surveys measure between 20 and 35 centimeters total length. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of 1.58 kilograms [Wwi = 1.58 kilograms] is thus attained only by a small fraction of the population, typically older individuals occupying deep pool habitats with abundant cover. Comparative data from the Colorado River drainage indicate that growth rates are strongly influenced by summer water temperatures, which frequently approach 30 °C, yet the species continues to feed and maintain condition at the moderate temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] that characterizes its optimal thermal niche. Life history trade-offs between growth, reproduction, and longevity are therefore mediated by local thermal regimes across the species' restricted geographic range.
